title: Cisco Duo Set User Status to Bypass 2FA
exclusions: Covers status changes made after collection starts; run the daily report of users in bypass status for the existing backlog.
evidence: Alert rows with before and after status, the user, and the administrator, plus the revert date agreed with the help desk.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In a test Duo account set an active test user's status to Bypass and save. After the next input interval the search returns one row with `old_status=Active` and `status=Bypass`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Set the same user back to Active. The `user_update` event is indexed but the status transition does not match, so no row is returned.

dataSources: `index=duo sourcetype=cisco:duo:activity` from the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) Duo input, Activity log type (`GET /admin/v2/logs/activity`).
app: Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, [Splunkbase 7404](https://splunkbase.splunk.com/app/7404)), Cisco Duo input. Replaces the deprecated Duo Splunk Connector (Splunkbase 3504, end of life 31 May 2026).
spl:
index=duo sourcetype="cisco:duo:activity" "action.name"=user_update
| spath input=target.details path=status output=status
| spath input=old_target.details path=status output=old_status
| search status=Bypass old_status=Active
| rename target.name as user access_device.ip.address as src_ip
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by user status old_status actor.name actor.type src_ip access_device.location.country
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
description: Finds Duo user updates where the account status changed from Active to Bypass, using the before and after details in the activity log. Shows the user, the administrator who made the change, and where the change was made from.
value: A user in Bypass status signs in with a password only, on every protected application, until someone changes it back. Attackers with admin access use it to make stolen passwords work, and help desks forget to revert it after a phone replacement.
implementation: Collect the Duo Activity log with the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) Duo input into `index=duo`. Alert on every change and pair it with a daily report of all users currently in bypass status.
visualization: Alert table: firstTime, user, actor.name, src_ip, access_device.location.country. Supporting single value: users currently in Bypass status.

references.title: Cisco Security Cloud App for Splunk User Guide

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Temporary help-desk bypass** — set for a user with a lost phone, with a ticket. Still alert, but route to the help desk to confirm the revert date.

2. **Directory sync** — status set by an automated sync shows `actor.type` as an integration rather than an administrator. Review the sync rule rather than the user.

**Suppression:** none recommended; every bypass change should have an owner.
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites
• Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, Splunkbase 7404) on the search heads and on the heavy forwarder or Splunk Cloud Inputs Data Manager that runs its modular inputs. It replaces the Duo Splunk Connector (Splunkbase 3504, end of life 31 May 2026); disable the old connector's inputs after cutover so events are not indexed twice.
• A Duo Admin API application created by an Owner-role administrator in the Duo Admin Panel under Applications > Protect an Application > Admin API. Record the integration key, secret key, and API hostname (`api-XXXXXXXX.duosecurity.com`), and grant it **Grant read log**.
• Outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) from the input host to the API hostname, and an accurate system clock on that host, because the Admin API signs every request with the current date.
• An index for Duo data (this page uses `index=duo`) and a role with `srchIndexesAllowed` on it for the identity and SOC teams.

Step 1 — Configure data collection
• In Cisco Security Cloud open Application Setup, choose the Cisco Duo card, and create an input with the integration key, secret key, and API hostname. Enable the Activity log type and set the index to `duo`.
• The input reads `GET /admin/v2/logs/activity` and writes `sourcetype=cisco:duo:activity`: nested JSON with `action.name`, `actor.name`, `actor.type`, `target.name`, `target.details`, `old_target.details`, `outcome.result`, and `access_device.*` (browser, OS, IP address, city, state, country).
• Run `index=duo sourcetype=cisco:duo:activity "action.name"=user_update | table _time actor.name target.name target.details old_target.details` and confirm both detail fields carry a `status` key.

Step 2 — Create the search and alert
```spl
index=duo sourcetype="cisco:duo:activity" "action.name"=user_update
| spath input=target.details path=status output=status
| spath input=old_target.details path=status output=old_status
| search status=Bypass old_status=Active
| rename target.name as user access_device.ip.address as src_ip
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by user status old_status actor.name actor.type src_ip access_device.location.country
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
```

Understanding this SPL
• `"action.name"=user_update` keeps user changes; the before and after states are JSON strings in `old_target.details` and `target.details`.
• The two `spath` calls pull `status` out of each JSON string; `status=Bypass old_status=Active` keeps only changes into bypass.
• `actor.name` and `actor.type` show whether an administrator or an integration made the change.

Step 3 — Validate
• Compare with the Duo admin console (Admin Panel): open the user under Users and confirm the status shows Bypass, and check the same change under Reports > Administrator Actions.
• Run `index=duo sourcetype=cisco:duo:activity | timechart span=1h count` over 7 days to confirm there are no collection gaps.

Step 4 — Operationalize
• Schedule every 15 minutes over the last 20 minutes; no throttling, because each change is a separate risk.
• The responder confirms with the user and the help desk, sets a revert date, and resets the user's password if the change is not recognized.
• Send to Enterprise Security as a finding on `user` when ES is in use.

Step 5 — Troubleshooting
• No Duo events and HTTP 401 in the input log under `$SPLUNK_HOME/var/log/splunk/duo_splunkapp/`: wrong secret key, an API hostname from a different Duo account, or clock skew on the input host.
• HTTP 403: the Admin API application is missing **Grant read log**.
• HTTP 429: Duo rate-limits the log endpoints. Make sure the deprecated 3504 connector and the 7404 input are not both polling the same Admin API application.
• Duplicate rows after migration: the 3504 connector and the 7404 input are both enabled for the same log type.
• Rows never match although bypass changes happened: your events record status in a different key. Inspect `target.details` on one raw event and adjust the `spath` path.
grandmaExplanation: We alert when someone switches off the second login check for a person's account, because then a password alone opens every app.
